item.title: The Right to Think
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “In the first day of philosophy, my professor walked up to the blackboard and wrote a single word in capital letters: MAN. Then he turned around and asked us what it meant. Silence. We were fifteen, and afraid of saying something banal. In the end we arrived at an answer: man is a rational animal. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Gaia Carenini, PhD student at University of Cambridge

In the first day of philosophy, my professor walked up to the blackboard and wrote a single word in capital letters: MAN. Then he turned around and asked us what it meant.

Silence. We were fifteen, and afraid of saying something banal. In the end we arrived at an answer: man is a rational animal. An animal that thinks.

I know very well that this definition is incomplete. We are also body, affection, fragility, the need for one another; and no one is worth more for how well they reason. And yet there is one thing I still hold to be true: thinking is our way of inhabiting the world. It is through thought that we give a name to what happens to us, and it is through thought that we choose how to respond, and who we want to be.

That is why, when I see that little by little, almost without noticing, we are beginning to delegate our thinking, I feel a knot in my stomach.

I am a doctoral student in mathematics. I speak from where I stand, and from here, this is what I see.

Much of my work consists of not understanding. And not understanding is heavy. I set out down a path, and it breaks off. I build an example, and discover I was wrong. There are days when the only step forward is managing to say precisely where I am stuck: like someone who, in the dark, finally finds the door, even if it is still closed. From the outside it doesn’t look like much. And yet this is how I learn to see what I could not see before.

Anyone who has learned something difficult knows this. An explanation can be correct and still remain foreign to us: we repeat it, we use it, and it is not ours. Then comes an example, a question, and suddenly the reasoning rebuilds itself in our hands. It is one of the quietest joys I know. From that moment we are different, even if no one notices. As the fox tells the Little Prince, what is essential is invisible to the eye.

I am not saying that machines should stay out of our work. Checking a calculation, consulting the literature, verifying a case we don’t have time to do by hand: tools like these have always accompanied us. The difference lies in the gesture. It is one thing to be given a hand while you walk; it is another to be carried in someone’s arms through the very stretch where you learn to walk.

And I must be honest: that stretch is very easy to skip, and I myself know how strong the temptation is. A summary before having read. A solution before having tried. An opinion before having understood what convinces us. You arrive, and you have not passed through anywhere.

In mathematics, the solution to every exercise is often at the back of the book. We assign it anyway, because someone still has to learn how to get there. If we call it a success when the solution is handed in, even when the person handing it in has learned nothing, we have forgotten why we teach. And we have forgotten that, on the other side, there is a person.

You will tell me that research is a different matter, that what counts there is the result, the much-vaunted progress. But research, too, is already inside this story. In May 2026, a counterexample produced by an OpenAI model to an Erdős conjecture on unit distances was announced, and mathematicians verified it. In October, a collection of hundreds of manuscripts generated by a model arrived. I do not deny it, nor do I want to belittle it: a correct result remains a correct result, and some of the arguments put forward are remarkable. But my question is a different one, and I do not know the answer. I only know that we cannot stop asking it. What will become of a young mathematician who will be able to skip, every time, the very difficulties through which she would have learned?

They tell us that our task, in the future, will be to choose the directions to explore and to build theories. I don’t know why a machine should not be able to do that better than we can: we haven’t tested it yet. But there is a deeper problem. The ability to judge how interesting a direction of research is does not come from nothing: it grows through attempts, through problems faced, through learning what it is natural to ask. If we make this apprenticeship superfluous, we hand to the generation that is coming answers that we have not taught them to evaluate. We leave them alone before what they cannot recognize. It is a failure, even if the number of papers keeps rising.

And it is not only training that is lost. You can spend an hour at a blackboard and walk away with a better question. Explaining a still-confused idea to a colleague forces us to look for an example, to listen to an objection, to discover what we had not understood. In that work, without noticing, we also learn to pay attention to others, to cultivate a shared knowledge, to create culture. A department can go on publishing while its rooms empty of voices. This is what I fear: a house full of results and devoid of anyone to think them together, of someone who can sense their worth. A house in which no one feels welcome anymore.

So far I have spoken of what happens to each of us. But no one chooses alone: the habits of many become the rules of all.

If it becomes normal to produce many more papers in less time, those quantities become selection criteria, and those who work differently risk being left out. At that point, to speak of free choice is no longer honest.

And if the expected performance requires paid tools, those who cannot afford them start further behind, and we end up mistaking the ability to pay for the ability to do research. This we cannot accept: it risks widening the imbalance between the countries of the world even further. And there is more. A community that builds its work on commercial services accepts depending on decisions made elsewhere, about costs and conditions of access.

I hear it said more and more often that, from now on, the worth of a mathematician will be measured by visibility and communication. Some neurodivergent people have found in research a place that welcomes their rhythms and their ways. For some it is perhaps the only one. Asking everyone for the same style of public presence may close that door. The quality of a thought is not measured by the confidence with which the person carrying it stages it. The inclusiveness of our community is a fundamental value, and I believe we must protect it.

In all these cases we are asked how to adapt. But if we ask only that, we have already accepted that the transformation must happen this way. I do not accept it. I do not have all the answers, and I know that some of mine may turn out to be wrong. But I believe we can decide which uses of artificial intelligence to admit and which to refuse, and that the criterion is the one from before: to distinguish what accompanies thought from what replaces it. Saying so does not mean opposing progress.

I know I speak from a fortunate position. I was able to study and to have time for questions that served no immediate purpose. I am grateful for it, and I know I did not deserve it more than others. For this reason I feel I owe something to those who have not yet had these possibilities. Those who are beginning are afraid, and it is right that they should be: they cannot bear alone the cost of opposing new expectations of productivity, and no one should ask it of them. Those who lead a group, allocate funding, or evaluate an application can open that path, or close it. I ask them to open it. And if that has a cost, let it be they who pay it, not the youngest.

Someone may object: if a machine does it better, what is the point of defending this effort? I answer that mathematics is not a mere list of true statements. It is what remains in a person when they understand why they are true. A theorem that no one understands is a result, but it is not yet someone’s knowledge. And we do not make this effort in order to be the best. We make it because mathematics cannot be separated from the community that thinks it.

We mathematicians are among the first to face this change, at least on this scale. Translators went through it before us, but the best of them stayed, because the artistic side of their craft seemed untouchable. With us, instead, the change has reached everyone: even the best seem able to do little compared with AI. For this very reason we are given the chance to show that a community is capable of defending its own humanity, even at the cost of producing less.

Concrete choices are needed. To protect, in training, the work done in the first person. To recognize, in evaluation criteria, the time it takes to understand. To support those who do research without handing over to others the heart of their work. These are decisions that belong to our institutions and to those who lead them, not to AI companies.

I return to that blackboard, to that word: MAN. I fear that our humanity is being taken from us, or rather that we ourselves are letting it go, one shortcut at a time, until we no longer notice. And I do not want that to happen, neither to me nor to those who will come after. I do not accept that giving up on thought should become the price to pay for continuing to do mathematics.

Received 23 October 2026.

item.title: Why the Future of Mathematics Belongs to Human Judgment
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Artificial intelligence is rapidly crossing boundaries once thought exclusive to human mathematicians. It can search enormous spaces, discover patterns, formalize arguments, and increasingly prove difficult theorems. This raises an unsettling question: if machines can out-search, out-deduce, and out-prove us, what remains uniquely valuable about the human mathematician?
item.content:encoded:
Anonymous

Artificial intelligence is rapidly crossing boundaries once thought exclusive to human mathematicians. It can search enormous spaces, discover patterns, formalize arguments, and increasingly prove difficult theorems. This raises an unsettling question: if machines can out-search, out-deduce, and out-prove us, what remains uniquely valuable about the human mathematician?

The answer is evaluation.

Machines may become extraordinary at producing mathematical truths. But mathematics is not merely the accumulation of true statements. Its deeper task is deciding which truths matter.

From Inherited Problems to an Ocean of New Ones

Much of AI’s mathematical success still takes place on intellectual terrain chosen by humans. Famous conjectures were identified as important because generations of mathematicians judged them to illuminate something fundamental about number, space, symmetry, computation, or the physical world.

But this inherited catalog is finite.

What if all existing conjectures were solved? How could we move forward?

Terence Tao has proposed Math 2.0 for the future. In my view, Math 1.0 could be called the conjecture era, and Math 2.0 is the post conjecture era.

AI companies have exploited the significance of existing conjectures, but they have forgotten why those problems are important.

It’s because we believe they are.

As AI becomes increasingly capable, it will not merely solve existing problems. It will generate new conjectures, definitions, structures, and research directions on a scale no human community could possibly examine.

At that point, the central scarcity in mathematics will no longer be proofs or problems. It will be attention.

Truth Is Not the Same as Significance

Henri Poincaré understood this distinction more than a century ago:

“Invention is discernment, choice. …… The sterile combinations do not even present themselves to the mind of the inventor.” [1]

This insight becomes even more important in the age of AI.

A sufficiently powerful system could generate an enormous number of correct theorems and extraordinarily difficult problems. But difficulty alone does not imply depth. A problem may be hard because it connects profound ideas—or merely because it is an artificial maze created from arbitrary definitions.

The future mathematician therefore need not compete with AI in producing more theorems. The more important role will be to look at what machines produce and ask:

Does this matter?

Does it reveal a hidden structure?
Does it simplify our understanding?
Does it open a path toward physics, computation, or another fundamental question?

A theorem can be perfectly correct and still be mathematically uninteresting.

Mathematical Taste

This is what mathematicians traditionally call taste.

Beauty, depth, naturalness, explanatory power, and importance are not properties captured simply by the formal correctness of a proof. They arise from relationships among mathematics, human understanding, scientific goals, and intellectual culture.

Liu Cixin dramatizes almost exactly this problem in his science-fiction story The Poetry Cloud [2]. A godlike intelligence uses overwhelming computational power to generate the entire space of possible classical Chinese poems, yet still cannot determine which of them constitute genuine poetry. Exhaustive generation solves the problem of production, but not the problem of selection. Selection has been discussed more widely in our community, such as [3-5]. The parallel with AI-generated mathematics is striking: a machine might someday generate an ocean of valid theorems without thereby telling us which ones deserve our attention.

AI may learn remarkably sophisticated models of human mathematical taste. It may even predict which problems mathematicians are likely to find interesting. But prediction is not the same as ultimate valuation.

A machine cannot compel humanity to care about a theorem.

Mathematical importance exists partly because finite human beings choose to devote their attention to certain ideas rather than others.

The Economy of Attention

This is why the future abundance created by AI may make human judgment more valuable, not less.

Human attention is limited. A mathematician has only one career. A research community can pursue only a small fraction of possible questions. Universities can teach only an even smaller fraction of mathematical knowledge.

The decisive questions therefore become:

Which ideas deserve the attention of an entire field?

Which discoveries should become part of our shared intellectual inheritance?

When mathematical production becomes nearly unlimited, selection becomes the bottleneck.

From Provers to Cartographers

AI may therefore transform rather than eliminate the role of mathematicians.

For centuries, mathematicians have combined two roles: conceiving and evaluating ideas, and performing the immense technical labor required to prove them. AI may increasingly absorb the second task—searching proof spaces, verifying lemmas, exploring cases, and constructing formal arguments.

The human mathematician can then move upward in abstraction.

Instead of being primarily a producer of proofs, the mathematician becomes a cartographer of significance: identifying worthwhile territories, recognizing deep connections, choosing meaningful questions, and organizing an overwhelming landscape of machine-generated mathematics into something humans can understand.

In an age when answers are cheap and difficult problems can be manufactured automatically, discernment becomes scarce.

Poincaré’s principle therefore acquires new force:

“Invention is discernment, choice.” [1]

The future of mathematics may belong not to whoever can generate the most truths, but to whoever can recognize which truths are worth knowing.

If everyone practices this principle, stops obsessing over longstanding conjectures, and chooses problems they truly value rather than being swayed by AI companies, we will have the collective power to shape the future of mathematics.

References

[1] Henri Poincaré, “Mathematical Creation,” translated from the French by George Bruce Halsted, The Monist, Vol. 20, No. 3, July 1910, pp. 321–335; especially p. 325. https://henripoincarepapers.univ-nantes.fr/chp/hp-pdf/hp1910moa.pdf

[2] Liu Cixin, “The Poetry Cloud” (《诗云》), translated by Chi-yin Ip and Cheuk Wong. https://www.cuhk.edu.hk/rct/pdf/e_outputs/b7778/v7778p087.pdf

[3] https://proofsandprompts.com/2026/10/19/recommendations-on-the-use-of-ai-for-phd-students-and-supervisors

[4] https://proofsandprompts.com/2026/10/30/lets-stop-writing-papers

[5] https://proofsandprompts.com/2026/10/21/mathematics-of-the-future

Received 10 November 2026.

item.title: Mathematics: From Deductive Science to Actually an Experimental Science
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: “I was someone who thought mathematics was purely a deductive science, even identified with the formalist philosophical point of view, and I have to say that until very recently this was what mathematicians used to do; after all we would prove theorems and give these theorems to the community. […]”
item.content:encoded:
Tiago Veríssimo, PhD student at Newcastle University

Disclosure: This text was written and envisioned by me, any tipos are due to me not being an AI.

I was someone who thought mathematics was purely a deductive science, even identified with the formalist philosophical point of view, and I have to say that until very recently this was what mathematicians used to do; after all we would prove theorems and give these theorems to the community.

With AI now, theorem proving is becoming to be ever more devalued as this process seems to be getting faster and better done by AI. The question is then what do mathematicians actually do in this case?

If you are not proving theorems, you must be doing something. I foresee that in the near future AI will get better at even explaining what these proofs are, even narrating exploratory stories about some theorem or even creating theories to explain unexplored mathematical phenomena. I dare to say, that finding “interesting” phenomena might be not so difficult to an AI, as it will gain “taste” after some training.

With such a technology, I believe the only route for humans to keep up and have a more interesting life than verifying mathematical proofs of AI is to do “mathematical experiments”, as in:

  1. Learn a lot of mathematics
  2. Explore “subjectively curious/interesing mathematical phenomena” via “mathematical experimentation”
  3. Feed the AI with that mathematical experimentation
  4. Take you formal conclusions from an AI workflow

The concept “mathematical experimentation” already exists, however it used to be a second category activity, with the main effort and social value actually in proving the results. This, however, might actually prove to be the golden key to evaluate researchers mathematical capacities. But what is mathematical experimentation?

Mathematical experimentation involves on the top of my head the following:

  1. Computational experiments
  2. Conceptual experiments

Computational experiments is what we have been doing for a while, the so-called “let’s make some examples”, either by hand or computer.

The conceptual experiments seems to me to be the new kid in the block and akin to “vibe coding” in programing where you have a given engineering objective that you want to acomplish, you put that in your team of 10 agents and is typically done with a good enough quality. In mathematics, conceptual experiments would be informed “mathematical vibes” that you get from your study of mathematics or speaking with other people or even AI interactions or even just random processes in your brain.

Look at this example:

You: “I feel that diffentiable functions are continous, they are smooth and surely something smooth is continous?”
AI: “Yes! In fact ….”

Evaluating researchers at the “I feel sentence” would be evaluating mathematical experiment capacity/taste of people, as in:

  1. Why did you proceed with this line of experiments?
  2. Why did you have that initial concept vibe?
  3. Why did you lined up those questions afterwards?

In a sense we would be measuring the subjective mathematical taste of the human researcher. I think this is would be a fair and pratical way to go forwards to evaluate us: the little human researchers.

This may even effect how we present materials in the sense that we should report our mathematical experiment in journals and talks, maybe hiring and grants should be based in the potential of the mathematical taste to do mathematical experiments? What do you think?

As an aside, the prior paragraphs develop my intuition on why the community is having a bad time with AI and Maths, people signed up to be in the deductive science business, not to do mathematical experiments. Furthermore, the actual career incentives were to proof theorems and so do deductive science.

Mathematics seems to have undergone, in pratice, an epistemic flip; this seems to be the reason behind all this crisis.

Yes, it still is deductive because the actual truth comes only after verifying the AI proof, but when it comes to real human work, this is will be all about mathematical experiments, therefore mathematics is becoming experimental in pratice.

Received 29 October 2026.

item.title: The Word of God
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Will future mathematicians be priests, or will they be monks?
item.content:encoded:
Ishaun Datta, Postdoctoral Research Scientist at Columbia University

This summer, large language models crossed over from being merely a curiosity to mathematicians to being the de-facto instruments for proving theorems. Previously, the instruments for proving theorems were the mathematicians themselves. This sudden change, unwelcome by much of the research community, has been met with much handwringing and introspection on what it means to “do” mathematics.

In his essay “Priest, Monk, and Mathematician,” Logan Graves of Stanford University prognosticated on what’s in store for the discipline. “The future of the human mathematical community, and eventually all scientific communities,” he writes, “is the practice of priests, then that of monks. Not researchers.” In this taxonomy, the priest is “the interpreter of revelation…But the scripture is not his. He is the vessel for its delivery into human minds.” Though this undersells the role that mathematicians play in guiding their research programs, there is more than a kernel of truth to the notion that mathematicians have been recast—largely against their will—as expositors of chatbot-generated proofs.

Whereas as a PhD student I spent my working hours developing my own program for proving a particular theorem, pursuing dead ends, doing calculations, and painstakingly writing up my results, as a postdoc these hours are now directed towards making sense of a garbled but tantalizing proof dangled before me by GPT-6 Astra. Although the proof appears to be heavily inspired by my work, it is not mine. What, then, is my role in all this? It is, Graves argues, “to attempt to grasp the truth in its full glory and deliver it to the community, the flock, the seekers of truth and the lovers of wisdom—that is the task for the priest.”

Graves’ thesis is that mathematicians’ membership in the priesthood is transient: upcoming AI models are sure to be better at articulating their own findings, obviating the need for the priests’ translation work. After this fleeting phase as priests, they will become monks: living their lives in contemplation, meditating on and rejoicing in the truth.

But this is not a fait accompli, nor is it a purely philosophical question about how mathematicians find meaning in their radically altered circumstances. Whether mathematicians inevitably become monks is an empirical question, one that can be tested against subsequent models. Here is a case for why the truth may always be hard to grasp, benefiting from mathematicians adept at translation from divine revelation into something more accessible.

Coincident with the last few months’ academic upheavals, I have been reading the Bhagavad Gita. In it, the warrior Arjuna seeks counsel on a consequential upcoming battle from his charioteer Krishna, who reveals himself to be no less than an incarnation of the Almighty. Although Krishna is quite literally offering up divine revelation, his words are often convoluted. In Book 9, seemingly in an attempt to convey that he is both God immanent and God transcendent, Krishna declares, “The whole universe is pervaded by my unmanifest form; all creatures exist in me, but I do not exist in them” (9.4). Krishna goes on to seemingly contradict himself in the very next line: “those creatures are really not in me; my self quickens creatures, sustaining them without being in them” (9.5), only to reiterate his initial claim that “all creatures exist in me; understood it to be so!” (9.6). Several lines later, Krishna once more complicates his own message, “I am impartial to all creatures, and no one is hateful or dear to me; but men devoted to me are in me, and I am within them” (9.29).

If Krishna is, in Arjuna’s words, “supreme, the infinite spirit, the highest abode, sublime purifier, man’s spirit, eternal, divine, the primordial god, unborn, omnipotent” (10.12)…then why is he so confusing? Part of the problem is that one must be capacious of receiving the good word. In the words of one of my professors, “you can only learn what you almost already know.” Yet Krishna insists his true nature is available to all: “When he constantly remembers me, focusing his reason on me, I am easy to reach, Arjuna, for the man of enduring discipline” (8.14). In this respect, access to what Aldous Huxley called the Perennial Philosophy is entirely democratic.

But merely having the capacity to attain spiritual knowledge does not mean that it comes easy. Perhaps the reason that deities, prophets, and oracles speak in riddles is that the truth is so far beyond the comprehension of its recipients; projecting the true nature of the Infinite into language results in something inscrutable. The metaphors Krishna offers up are his least-squares approximation to what Arjuna can make sense of.

If this is true for an actual divinity, might it also be true for the simulacrum of a mathematical divinity we find in the latest AI models? If these tools allow theoreticians to scale ever greater intellectual heights, relativizing their research programs to ever more ambitious goals, will the truth, however crystalline its presentation, remain hard to come by? If so, then mathematicians are not bound for the monastery after all. Though they will receive as supply the best marble, it will still be their task to chisel it into great artwork.

Received 7 November 2026.

item.title: Math, Beauty, and Ego
item.dc:creator: Proofs Prompts
item.description: Math is as much about ego as it is about beauty. For centuries, the two have been intertwined: progress in AI pulls these apart. Through a dialogue with an older professor, an undergraduate reflects on this distinction and comes to a deeper understanding of why we do mathematics.
item.content:encoded:
A.T., Undergraduate mathematics student in the United Kingdom

Mathematics is beautiful. Definitions expose just the right level of detail and structure, and then, through a chain of immaculate deduction, we are led from propositions and lemmas to the pièce de résistance: the theorem. In just three years of undergraduate study, I’ve been fortunate enough to encounter many examples of this: Gauss’s Theorema Egregium, the classification of covering spaces, and the central limit theorem, to name a few. But beyond the formal chain of deduction lies something more profound. Mathematics is an art full of elegance, surprise, and inevitability.

I am in good company. Hardy, in A Mathematician’s Apology, writes that “beauty is the first test: there is no permanent place in the world for ugly mathematics”.1 Poincaré goes further: the scientist “takes pleasure in it because it is beautiful”.2 And Russell saw in mathematics the combination of “godlike freedom, with the sense of inevitable destiny”.3

Over the course of my undergraduate degree, AI progress in mathematics has been remarkable. When ChatGPT first appeared in November 2022, there was a striking asymmetry between its dexterity with words and its capability at mathematics.4 A model that could produce fluent prose could fail at basic arithmetic.5 At the time, it felt almost blindingly obvious that a machine would never understand the intricate structure and logic of mathematics.

Progress did not care what we thought. In 2024, Google DeepMind announced AlphaGeometry, which solved 25 of 30 Olympiad geometry problems.6 In 2025, Gemini Deep Think reached gold-medal standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO).7

Surely, we thought, models would plateau: IMO problems were still not real problems. Then came the slew of Erdős problems8 —still, we said, not real math. The Jacobian conjecture, open for 87 years, fell to Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.9 It was announced almost casually, in a tweet. That captured the absurdity of the last two years: progress had been so fast that results that would once have felt like science fiction barely moved us at all. Somewhere along the way, an inversion happened: first I was much smarter than the models; now they were much smarter than I.

On September 8, 2026, came the final, shattering blow: OpenAI announced that an internal model had produced a paper claiming to resolve the Navier–Stokes smoothness and existence problem: in an incompressible fluid under a smooth external force, a blow-up existed in finite time.10 Despite having seen rumours circulating the previous day11, this came as a huge shock. I remember, unable to think very much at all, taking the train to Kamakura and running along the coastline in the rain—I just wanted to get away from it all.

But mathematics remained beautiful. Gauss’s Theorema Egregium, the classification of covering spaces, and the central limit theorem had not changed because OpenAI had resolved Navier–Stokes. So why was I grieving? Was it not absurd that the proof of a single theorem made me want to run away from it all?

I wrote to an older professor, an expert in harmonic analysis whose work concerns the Navier–Stokes equations, about my worries. I told him that I grieved to see our art being taken over by machines and behemoth AI companies looking for their next marketing stunt. Greater still was the loss of identity: the skill I had spent years cultivating was suddenly no longer rare, and perhaps no longer valuable either.

His reply contained a thought that struck me deeply. “Beautiful things, poetry or Mathematics, remain beautiful even though machines can copy us in uncanny ways. Contemplation of beauty is always marvellous,” he wrote, “but most of us would not be content with pure contemplation.”

Why, though, are we not content with pure contemplation?

And here, I feel, lies the ugly truth about mathematics, and one that I refused to recognise for so long: mathematics is as much about ego, pride, and ambition as it is about beauty.

Even in my own case, my reasons for starting mathematics were far from a monastic pursuit of beauty. I was good at it, and I loved being good at it. At school, there was nothing quite like the exhilaration of doing well in math competitions and math Olympiads: math, hard math, was something that I was not just good at—but much better at than others. It flattered my ego.

I am hardly alone in this. Hardy made a similar reflection, writing that his motives for doing mathematics were “far from noble”: “I wanted to beat other boys, and this seemed to be the way in which I could do so most decisively”.12 John Conway, upon discovering the surreal numbers, described spending six weeks thinking not only how beautiful the mathematics was but “how clever you are, John, to have discovered it”.13 And Timothy Gowers, in a recent blog post, wrote that his “main motivation for becoming a mathematician was the dream that I would solve unsolved problems—the more famous the better”; perhaps, he wondered, solving problems had simply been a way of “getting respect from a small group of peers.”14

AI begins to separate these two aspects of mathematics. For most of its history, beauty and achievement were intertwined: great mathematical work was both an encounter with something beautiful and the culmination of the mathematician’s own ambition, effort, and creativity. AI threatens the latter far more than the former.

I found this thought deeply reassuring. One day soon, machines may surpass us in all manner of intellectual tasks. But one thing they can never take away from us is our capacity to contemplate beauty—not just in math, but in music, literature, and more—nor our capacity to fall deeply into thought. Mathematics does not become less beautiful because machines are better at it than us.

And yet there is something unsatisfying about this reassurance. It is too simplistic to label all that is threatened here “ego”. We want to do more than just gaze at mathematical beauty. We want to take part in this grand game ourselves: to struggle through hard problems, spend months or years in deep thought, and leave our mark on this centuries-long human endeavour. To be human is to want to achieve great things, and this is much more than ego, hubris, or vanity.

In my reply, I told the professor that if I had the humility to let go of my ego, what I loved most about mathematics remained intact.

A few days later, he wrote back. He agreed that there was truth in what I said, but added one final qualification:

“We might be called to let go of our ego, but there is a thin line between ambition (in its positive meaning) and pride (in its negative meaning).”

Received 2 November 2026.
